To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a 1D flamelet generated manifold is able to model the main features of premixed counter flow flames with unit Lewis numbers.

(1) the FGM method can model the effects of flame stretch accurately; (2) the FGM manifold should be constructed using one progress variable for unit Lewis number mixtures and one additional controlling variable if the Lewis number is not unity; and (3) the FGM manifolds can be used to model non premixed flames as well, if the progress variable is chosen appropriately
a manifold with one progress variable can be used to simulate premixed flames if the Lewis numbers of the reactants are equal to one.

the development of a new method for the simulation of turbulent combustion.
the development of a new method for the simulation of premixed turbulent combustion.
the development of the FGM approach and the validation of its accuracy in the modelling of premixed counterflows.

a manifold with two controlling variables is required to model the effect of flame stretching on the main features of premixed methane/ air counterflow flames.
the FGM method with two controlling progress variables is able to model premixed counterflow methane/air flames with Lewis numbers deviating significantly from unity.
for the premixed counterflow case the FGM method can be used to model the effects of flame stretch on a 1D flamelet manifold.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the FGM method with one progress variable and a unit Lewis number gives a good description of the main effects of the flame stretch, and that a two progress variable manifold gives a very good description when non unit Lewis numbers and composition changes are considered.
in the FGM method the flame stretch is taken into account by the use of 1D flamelets.
the FGM method can be used to model counterflow flames with reasonable accuracy. However, the manifold should contain at least two controlling variables.
